title: The map of machine learning
html:
Purpose. When you meet a new technique, you should know which family it belongs to and what kind of problem it solves. This chapter is the map. Later chapters fill in the territory.

Key ideas

  • Supervised learning learns from examples with the right answer. Its two tasks are regression (predict a number) and classification (predict a category).
  • Unsupervised learning has no answers and finds structure: clusters, unusual cases, simpler descriptions.
  • Reinforcement learning learns from rewards by trial and error.
  • The first question to ask about any problem is: do I have the right answers for past cases?

Read the map from left to right. Machine learning splits into three ways to learn, each into types, each with its models. Course 1 of Ng's specialization starts at the highlighted Regression box. Course 2 adds neural networks and trees, and course 3 adds clustering, anomaly detection and reinforcement learning.

2.1 Supervised learning

In supervised learning each training example is a pair: an input x and the right answer y (the label). The algorithm learns the mapping from x to y, so that it can predict y for an input it has never seen. Ng says that about 99% of the economic value created by machine learning today comes from this family.

It comes in two tasks:

  • Regression predicts a number from infinitely many possible values. A house price from its size. A monthly loan cost from the amount and the term.
  • Classification predicts a category from a small set. Spam or not spam. A tumour that is benign (0) or malignant (1). The classes need not be numbers (cat or dog), and there can be more than two (Gmail's tabs: primary, social, promotions). With two inputs, the algorithm draws a boundary line between the classes.

2.2 Unsupervised learning

The data has inputs only. Nobody tells the algorithm what the answers are, so it looks for structure by itself. Ng's examples: Google News puts articles that share words (panda, twins, zoo) into one group; researchers group people by DNA activity; DeepLearning.AI found three learner segments (growing skills, developing a career, staying updated). The three main tasks:

  • Clustering: group similar examples.
  • Anomaly detection: find unusual examples, such as fraud.
  • Dimensionality reduction: compress many features into a few while keeping most of the information.

2.3 Reinforcement learning

An agent takes actions in an environment and receives rewards or penalties. It learns which actions earn the most reward over time. Famous examples: checkers (Samuel), Go (AlphaGo), and the training of reasoning LLMs, which were rewarded for correct answers. It is rare in lending, because you cannot let a model try random loans to see what happens, but it matters for understanding how modern LLMs are made.

2.4 Side by side

Supervised Unsupervised Reinforcement
The data Inputs x with right answers y Inputs x only An environment that gives rewards
The goal Learn x to y, then predict y for a new x Find groups, patterns, oddities Choose actions that earn the most reward
Tasks Regression, classification Clustering, anomaly detection, dimensionality reduction Control, games, tuning LLMs
Loan example Monthly cost of an offer (regression); offer accepted or not (classification) Applicant segments; an unusual application Rare; a pricing policy learned from simulation

2.5 Choosing the family

Question Answer Family and task
Do I have the right answers for past cases? Yes, and the answer is a number Supervised, regression
Yes, and the answer is a category Supervised, classification
No, and I want groups Unsupervised, clustering
No, and I want the odd ones out Unsupervised, anomaly detection
No, and I have too many columns Unsupervised, dimensionality reduction
Must it choose actions and learn from their results? Yes Reinforcement learning

Quick tests from Ng's quiz: spam filtering and diabetes prediction are supervised (the answers are known); grouping news articles and finding market segments are unsupervised.

2.6 Self-supervised learning

Beyond the videos. There is a fourth label you will meet when reading about LLMs: self-supervised learning. The training data comes with no human labels, but the labels are made from the data itself. An LLM reads a sentence with the next word hidden and learns to predict it. The "right answer" is simply the next word of the text. This lets models learn from the entire internet without anyone labelling it.

Loan example. A table of 40,000 past offers with a column Accepted (yes or no) is supervised classification data. The same table without that column can still be clustered into customer types, but the groups come with no names and you must interpret them.

Common mistakes

  • Calling a clustering result a classification. Clustering has no known classes. It invents groups, and you give them meaning afterwards.
  • Using regression for a yes or no question just because the labels are 0 and 1 (Chapter 9 explains why that goes wrong).

Check yourself

  • Is "predict whether a customer repays" regression or classification? Why?
  • Is "find groups of similar loan applicants" supervised or unsupervised?
  • Give one loan example of anomaly detection.
  • What is the label in supervised learning?
Show answers

(1) Classification: the answer is a category (repays or not). (2) Unsupervised: there is no right answer to learn from. (3) Flagging an application whose pattern differs from all previous ones, as a fraud check. (4) The right answer y that comes with each training example.
